newsitem.title: JAPAN: U.S. defence secretary in Japan for security talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. defence secretary in Japan for security talks.

text.p: The U.S. Defence Secretary arrived in Tokyo on Monday to seek assurances of "non-combat" support from Japanese forces in a Korean conflict and to urge Japan to join Washington's costly missile defence initiative.

William Cohen said he would raise the matters with Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and top officials over the next two days, but stressed he was aware of the sensitivity needed because of Japan's constitution, which forbids the use of military force except to defend itself.
Cohen, also on a mission to dampen down opposition to U.S. forces in Japan, is making his first visit to Washington's chief ally in Asia since taking over as defence secretary.

"We will discuss regional security issues and the role that Japan and the United States will play," he told reporters aboard his aircraft, flying from Hawaii on a trip that will also take him to South Korea.
Cohen said the Tokyo talks would include "ways in which, should a (Korean) crisis develop, Japan's forces could be helpful in lending support in various ways."
"But it would be supportive in a humanitarian aspect and perhaps NEO (non-combat evacuation order) operations or other types of activities which would not be combat oriented."

The two countries are negotiating an update of their 1978 joint "defence guidelines" for security cooperation, a matter which will also be discussed by Hashimoto and U.S. President Bill Clinton at a Washington meeting later this month.
The United States wants firm assurances that U.S. forces could use bases in Japan for operations or transportation in case of a new war in Korea.
Japanese forces also might help evacuate civilians threatened by such a conflict. U.S. officials said.
On another security issue, Washington is spending billions of dollars to develop missiles, lasers and other weapons which might be used to destroy attacking missiles in flight.

Cohen dines with Defence Agency chief Fumio Kyuma on Monday night and meets Hashimoto on Wednesday for talks including Japan's internal debate on whether to commit money and technology to the U.S. "Theatre Missile Defence" effort.
"I will raise this issue of TMD," Cohen said, adding that Japan should be aware that it could face danger from missile development in North Korea.
"We would hope that Japan would share in the development of these types of technologies, but that's of course a decision that the Japanese will have to make."

Another U.S. official, who asked not to be named, said Japan had financial and other reservations about the need for missile defence, but advanced Japanese technology in missile detection sensors would be a boon to the programme.

Cohen praised Hashimoto's efforts to maintain support by the Japanese for the presence of 47,000 U.S. troops in Japan, more than half of whom are on the island of Okinawa. He said he would assure the prime minister of Washington's determination to keep 100,000 American troops in the western Pacific indefinitely.

"I will be conveying that we regard the Pacific region as the most dynamic in the world today and that our bilateral relationship with Japan is key to maintaining that dynamic relationship," Cohen said.
Cohen's arrival comes as Hashimoto is pushing through new legislation to force private landowners, including those on Okinawa, to continue leasing their land for U.S. bases.
In September 1995, the rape of a 12-year-old Okinawan schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen triggered public outcry against the huge U.S. military presence on the island.
